title: ISC2 CISSP-ISSEP
summary: The Information Systems Security Engineering Professional (ISSEP) is a concentration exam from ISC2 for holders of the Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP) who work on systems engineering. It sits at an advanced level and suits security engineers, systems engineers, architects and consultants who build security into a system from the first requirement to final disposal. It proves to an employer that you can run the engineering process properly, manage risk across a system lifecycle, and produce the documentation that certification and accreditation bodies expect. The exam covers five published domains, from engineering foundations and risk management through design, secure operations, and the disposal or transition of a system, using multiple choice items that test process judgement. It leads to roles such as security engineer, systems security architect, and programme security lead. This is an independent study guide that is not official ISC2 material; confirm the current outline with the vendor before booking.

beginner.definition: The Information Systems Security Engineering Professional (ISSEP) is an advanced certification from ISC2. It is open only to people who already hold the Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP). It is about building security into a system during its design and engineering, not about fixing it afterwards.
beginner.whyItMatters: It costs far less to design security in than to add it later. Engineers who can do this are in demand for large projects. This certificate proves that you know the whole system lifecycle and the paperwork that goes with it. It supports senior engineering and consultancy roles. It also shows that you can work with project managers and customers, not only with code.
howItWorks: Confirm that you hold the Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP) and meet the rules for a concentration exam.
Read the official ISC2 exam outline and note the five domains and the tasks in each one.
Study the systems engineering process, from needs and requirements to design, testing and disposal.
Learn how risk is assessed and accepted across the life of a system.
Practise questions that describe a project stage and ask for the correct engineering action.
The exam is multiple choice and separate from the core exam, so allow several months of study.
beginner.example: Think about buying a new payroll system for a government office. An engineer who understands this certification does not start with the software. They first write down the security needs, such as who may approve a payment and how records are kept. Then they check each design choice against those needs, test the system, and plan how the old system and its data will be destroyed at the end. That orderly path is what the ISSEP exam rewards.
takeaways: The certification follows a system from first requirement to final disposal.
Learn the engineering process and the documents it produces, not only the technology.
You must hold the Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP) before you take this exam.

objectives: Apply a recognised systems security engineering process to a real project
Write security requirements that can be tested and traced through a design
Assess and treat risk at each stage of a system's life
Check that a design meets its security requirements before it goes live
Plan secure operation, maintenance and change for a deployed system
Prepare a system and its data for safe disposal or transfer

chapters.title: Systems security engineering foundations
objectives: Describe how security engineering fits into the wider systems engineering process
Gather stakeholder needs and turn them into clear security requirements
Apply standards and frameworks that guide secure system development
Explain the roles of the engineer, the customer and the accreditor
Trace each requirement from its source through design and testing

chapters.title: Risk management in systems engineering
objectives: Identify threats and weaknesses at each stage of the lifecycle
Score risk and decide which treatment is appropriate
Track risk as the design changes and record who accepted it
Link technical risk to the mission the system must support
Report risk clearly to non technical decision makers

chapters.title: Security planning, design and implementation
objectives: Choose security controls that satisfy the agreed requirements
Design the security architecture for the system and its interfaces
Plan verification and testing that proves each control works
Prepare the documentation needed for accreditation or approval
Manage design changes without weakening the security position

chapters.title: Secure operations, maintenance and sustainment
objectives: Operate the system within its approved security baseline
Manage patching, upgrades and configuration change safely
Monitor for incidents and respond using the agreed plan
Keep the risk assessment and accreditation current over time
Plan for supply chain and supplier changes during operation

chapters.title: Secure disposal and transition
objectives: Decide when a system should be retired or replaced
Plan the secure transfer of data and services to a new system
Destroy or sanitise media so that data cannot be recovered
Update records and agreements when a system is removed
Capture lessons from the retired system for future projects
